According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Magnetic V-Blocks market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global Magnetic V-Blocks market is entering a period of sustained expansion, with demand projected to rise at a compound annual growth rate of 5.7% between 2026 and 2035. This growth is underpinned by the accelerating adoption of automated quality-control systems, the expansion of semiconductor fabrication capacity, and the tightening of dimensional tolerances across precision engineering sectors. Magnetic V-Blocks, as precision workholding devices, are integral to machining, inspection, and assembly operations where ferromagnetic workpieces must be secured at exact angles. The market is relatively compact but structurally critical, with demand closely tied to capital investment in automated inspection lines, coordinate measuring machines, and high-precision manufacturing cells. As end users shift from manual setups to fully integrated workholding solutions, the demand for premium-grade blocks with enhanced magnetic stability, wear resistance, and calibration traceability is growing. The market is also benefiting from the modernization of metrology standards, particularly the adoption of ISO 10360 guidelines for CMM accessories, which is aligning procurement specifications globally. However, the market faces challenges from volatile rare-earth magnet feedstock prices and the need for extended supplier qualification cycles. This report provides a comprehensive analysis of market size, demand structure, supply dynamics, trade flows, pricing, and competitive landscape, with a forecast horizon extending to 2035. The baseline scenario for the Magnetic V-Blocks market points to steady growth through 2035, with the market index rising from 100 in 2025 to approximately 178 by 2035. This expansion is supported by several structural factors. First, the proliferation of automated quality assurance in electronics and semiconductor manufacturing is driving demand for high-precision workholding solutions that can maintain repeatable clamping force within ±2% across temperature variations. Second, the trend toward hardened tool-steel and ceramic-coated blocks is extending replacement intervals, but also increasing unit value, supporting revenue growth. Third, the integration of Magnetic V-Blocks with vision inspection systems and CMM fixtures is raising technical specifications, creating a premium segment that is expected to grow faster than the overall market. Fourth, regional standardization initiatives in metrology are harmonizing procurement requirements, benefiting suppliers with certified compliance packages. The market is also witnessing a shift toward modular and integrated systems with control interfaces, which offer greater flexibility and automation compatibility. However, growth is tempered by supply-side constraints, including the volatility of neodymium and cobalt prices, which can swing 15-25% over 12-month periods, and the 6-12 month qualification lead times for new vendors. Import dependence remains above 60% in most regions outside East Asia and Western Europe, prompting multi-sourcing strategies. Overall, the market is expected to grow at a CAGR of 5.7% from 2026 to 2035, with the premium segment outperforming standard industrial sets. In industrial automation, Magnetic V-Blocks are used to secure ferromagnetic parts during automated machining, grinding, and inspection. The segment is expanding as manufacturers adopt flexible manufacturing systems that require quick changeovers and precise positioning. Demand is driven by the need for repeatable clamping force within ±2% to ensure consistent quality in high-volume production. By 2035, the integration of V-blocks with robotic loading and vision systems will increase, requiring blocks with embedded sensors or RFID tags for traceability. Key demand-side indicators include capital expenditure on automation equipment, robot density in manufacturing, and the number of new automated inspection lines. The trend toward modular workholding systems is also boosting demand for interchangeable magnetic inserts and wear pads, which are consumables with a shorter replacement cycle. In electronics and optical systems, Magnetic V-Blocks are used for holding small ferromagnetic components during precision assembly, alignment, and inspection. The segment is growing rapidly as consumer electronics, medical devices, and optical instruments require tighter tolerances and cleaner handling. Demand is driven by the proliferation of automated optical inspection (AOI) systems and the need for stable, vibration-free workholding during high-magnification inspection. By 2035, the trend toward miniaturization will increase the demand for micro-sized V-blocks with extremely flat surfaces and low magnetic leakage. The adoption of ceramic-coated blocks is particularly strong here to prevent particle contamination. Demand-side indicators include global electronics production indices, semiconductor packaging volumes, and the number of precision optical assembly lines. The shift toward electric vehicles and advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) is also creating new applications for V-blocks in sensor assembly and calibration. The segment is expanding as semiconductor fabs increase capacity and adopt advanced packaging technologies like chiplets and 3D stacking. Demand is driven by the need for vibration-free clamping during high-resolution metrology and lithography processes. The adoption of ISO 10360 standards for CMM accessories is particularly relevant here, as semiconductor manufacturers require certified calibration. Chinook Observer: What’s your favorite thing to fish for? Kris Griffith: “I like salmon and tuna, for different reasons. I like trolling. I think of salmon as being an elegant, proud fish, then tuna are just eating machines — so aggressive and really fun. I find a deeper spiritual connection [with salmon fishing]. Tuna is a primal battle to catch as many and the biggest as I can.” Observer: Is there a day that stands out as your most memorable fishing day? Griffith: “Yes, it was the second tuna trip I ever did on this boat. The first trip, we filled a couple totes with fish, then the second trip it was just me, by myself. I ended up filling about five tons in three days, one of the hardest three days of work that I’ve ever had. “And it was just such an accomplishment… to buy this boat, then almost die on it immediately, then rebuild it from the ground up, take it down to the bare wood and go through it with a fine-tooth comb… try to build my trust up on this boat and just work on it, work on it by myself, then go out and be successful the first time alone… To be able to fill the boat on the second trip and really make it happen, to make my pipe dream a reality like, ‘Wow, I’m really doing it.’” Thank you for reading the Chinook Observer.Subscribe to get Unlimited Access to our website.

title: Drake Turns Kick Stream Into a 20-v-1 Dating Show, Warns Rap Rivals His ‘Pen Isn’t Dry’ - Rolling Stone Australia
content: The best in culture from a cultural icon. Subscribe now for more from the authority on music, entertainment, politics and pop culture. Inside the rapper’s chaotic Kick stream, featuring Lena the Plug, an Hermès giveaway, and apparent subliminals involving Lil Yachty and Roc Nation On Saturday, Drake continued his ongoing forays into the world of content creators, hosting a stream on Kick, which is affiliated with Stake, the crypto gambling company Drake is partnered with, which saw the rapper, fresh off the release of three new albums, flirting with a goth streamer, gifting out birkins, and sending not so subtle warnings to the rest of the rap game, noting that his “pen isn’t dry.” The roughly three-hour broadcast marked the ninth anniversary of Stake, the online crypto casino that has sponsored Drake’s livestreams for years. The company announced the stream with an Instagram post advertising more than $1 million in cash and prize giveaways, including a $50,000 grand prize for one viewer. During the actual stream, things moved quickly beyond gambling, turning into something closer to a chaotic Drake variety show. Drake also used the opening portion of the stream to reflect on his recent releases, patting himself on the back a little for dropping three projects at once. He also has a warning for anyone considering taking more shots in his direction. “These guys are dropping albums, like hello and goodbye, and careful with that reply ’cause the pen isn’t dry,” he said. Drake has been, of late, repping his Canadian upbringing pretty heavily, so it isn’t much of a surprise that he was joined by NELK co-founder Kyle Forgeard, who presented Drake with an SNL-style take on the popular 20-v-1 dating-show format. The women cycled through conversations with the rapper, who eventually had to choose one to “wife,” another to hook up with and a third to make his best friend. The proceedings included a contestant asking Drake to demonstrate his favorite sexual position and an appearance from adult-content creator Lily Phillips, who went viral in late 2024 after a documentary chronicled her having sex with 101 men in a single day. Phillips announced that she was “rebranding as Drake’s wife.” The final three were influencer Jordyn Lucas, adult-film star Lena the Plug, and goth streamer Pinkchyu. Drake placed Lucas in the best-friend category and gave her $25,000 and a Birkin. Lena, who briefly removed her wedding ring after hugging Drake, received $25,000 and an all-expenses-paid trip reportedly to New Zealand. In something of a callback to his September 2025 appearance on Bobbi Althoff’s podcast Not This Again, where he said his destiny was to end up with a “goth baddie,” Drake leaned into his self-described type by giving Pinkchyu the “wife” designation. This after she had him bark on command. The night also fueled more rap beef speculation. Drake floated the idea of holding Stake’s 10th-anniversary broadcast next year on a yacht, then quickly added that he hates boats. Given rumors that he and Lil Yachty, better known as Boat, have fallen out, Akademiks, naturally livestreaming Drake’s livestream, wondered whether the remark was a subliminal shot. Drake denied it. In another moment already being heavily clipped online, Drake joked that the “Roc Nation subpoenas” were “about to be cleared.” The remark appeared to refer to a recent What’s The Dirt video speculating that Roc Nation had played some role in the federal class action targeting Drake and Stake. Nine days earlier, a Virginia judge had ordered the plaintiffs’ claims against Stake into private arbitration and paused the remainder of the case, including the claims naming Drake. The stream was the latest example of the new norms of online video, where viral clips can quickly come to flood the feed thanks in no small part to companies like Kick’s well-reported army of clippers, dutifully turning each newsworthy moment into viral fodder. Get your daily dose of everything happening in Australian/New Zealand music and globally. It ultimately worked like a compressed version of Drake’s current internet strategy—especially the giving away huge sums of money part. Yet another signal that Drake sees real value in this emerging media ecosystem. On “First Person Shooter,” from 2023’s For All the Dogs, he famously rapped, “My youngins richer than you rappers and they all stream,” and has since enmeshed himself even more deeply in the world of streamers and content creators. During this year’s Streamer University, hosted by Kai Cenat, Drake delivered a prerecorded address to attendees and left care packages in their rooms stocked with cologne, Nocta clothing, Pokémon cards and other gifts. “I hope you learn something,” he told the class. “I hope you’re able to teach each other things.” In This Article: akademiks, Drake, Kai Cenat, Lil Yachty, Roc Nation

title: John Dobson on how 'feedback' from Stormers v All Blacks clash could help Springboks - Planet Rugby
content: All Blacks scrum-half Cortez Ratima kicks for touch and Stormers boss John Dobson looks on (inset). After initially exchanging information with the Springboks ahead of Friday’s clash with the All Blacks, the Stormers will now provide feedback to the world champions on the men in black. That was the word from Stormers director of rugby John Dobson after the All Blacks clinched a hard-fought victory over his troops in their tour opener at the DHL Stadium. Dobson revealed that the discussions with Springboks head coach Rassie Erasmus and his coaching staff were fruitful and forms part of a developing alignment between South Africa’s United Rugby Championship teams and the world champions in the build-up to Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry’s four-Test series with the All Blacks. The Springboks and All Blacks will face off in three matches in South Africa – in Johannesburg (twice) and Cape Town, before Baltimore hosts the fourth and final Test on September 12. Dobson opened up on initial discussions between the Stormers and Springboks’ coaching camps and revealed that a follow-up conversation is now set to take place. “We (the Stormers and Bok coaches) had a chat last week, just normal alignment,” he told reporters after Friday’s clash with the All Blacks. “I think it’s quite clever and I’ll probably give feedback (on the match). “But we are South African teams and I think they’d be interested to know how we experienced the clash, I know they will. “So we’ll give some feedback on what we found. I don’t think that’s unusual, but yeah, we shared some thoughts during the week and it actually was really useful. title: V-twin cruiser with automatic transmission slides under $6,000 - New Atlas
content: Typically, if you’re in the market for a cruiser with an automatic transmission, you’d have precious few options. The closest mainstream offering is Honda's Rebel 1100 DCT, which starts at around US$10,400 – and even that swaps the traditional V-twin for a parallel-twin engine. If you insist on a genuine V-twin and an automatic gearbox, you're effectively out of luck. Step in the Coaster 407: a genuine V-twin cruiser with an automatic transmission (AMT) from Spanish motorcycle manufacturer Rieju, based in Figueres, Catalonia. And it only requires you to spend about half as much, too. I have to point out that the motorcycle appears to be entirely Chinese-made, including its design. Rieju has simply stuck its badge on the tank, and voila, you have a brand new motorcycle “born” in the West. Do I like that practice? Not really. But do I get it? Absolutely. Rieju is hardly the first bikemaker to hop on this trend. Brands like Brixton, AJS, Mash, and Benelli (which is actually Chinese-owned) have either embraced Chinese OEMs as manufacturing partners or simply rebadged existing platforms. Starting with the engine, it is a water-cooled, 8-valve, 385cc V-twin – not a 407 as its name suggests. It’s a Euro 5+ compliant engine, producing 34.6 hp at 8,250 rpm and peak torque of 26.5 lb.ft (36 Nm) at 4,500 rpm. That’s quite a drop from the A2 class limit of 48 hp, but it’s not too bad considering you’re able to max out at 96 mph (155 km/h). But perhaps the biggest selling point of this motorcycle is its automatic transmission. You do get a clutch lever, but there’s no traditional gear shifter at your foot. Either the shifting through the six gears is fully automatic on the AMT on the Coaster 407, or you can simply engage the clutch and shift via paddles on the left handlebar. It rolls on multi-spoke cast aluminum wheels, measuring 19 inches at the front and 17 inches at the rear. You get enclosed telescopic forks at the front offering 4.7 in (120 mm) of travel, while a hidden shock at the rear offers a meager 2.5 in (65 mm) of travel. Braking is via one disc per wheel – 300 mm with NISSIN dual-piston caliper at the front and 240 mm at the rear, although ABS comes as standard. The Coaster 407 even features traction control (TCS), a digital display with connectivity, a keyless entry system, and two USB ports (Type-A and -C), as some standard features. Now let's not forget who this motorcycle is for: beginners and riders moving up the ladder from smaller, single-cylinder bikes. And for that purpose, the numbers look very appropriate. A rider-friendly seat height of only 27.1 in (690 mm) means even beginners would be able to feel confident on the bike. And a weight of 396 lb (180 kg) without fuel means it's one of the lighter cruisers out there. Speaking of which, we are talking about a cruiser here. The long, low silhouette, kicked-out front end, teardrop fuel tank and stubby rear fender tick all the right boxes in that regard. The V-twin sits proudly on display rather than being buried beneath acres of plastic, complemented by twin slash-cut exhausts and a belt final drive that do lend the bike a clean look. And unlike other chrome-laden options on the market, the Coaster 407 takes a far more restrained approach to its styling. You get blacked-out engine cases, dark-finished wheels, and fork legs and exhausts, with only subtle metallic accents breaking up the monotony. A generous wheelbase, low-slung seat, and gently raked fork create the classic "long and low" cruiser profile, with the compact tail section keeping the bike from appearing overly stretched. In Spain, the Rieju Coaster 407 has been priced at €4,961. That’s around US$5,726 per direct conversion. A sub-€5,000 MSRP is also being widely touted for other parts of Europe. However, I see it as highly unlikely that it will make its way outside of Europe to markets like the USA, Canada and Australia. That’s too bad because the strongest compliment I can pay the Coaster 407 is that it doesn't scream "budget motorcycle." It looks rather handsome and well-balanced for what’s essentially a white-labeled Chinese product. But then again, what’s not a white-labeled Chinese product these days?

At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. Just days before Nigel Farage takes on Count Binface in the Clacton by-election, a pilot traced the shape of a bin with their flightpath near the coastal town. According to flight tracking data from Flightradar24, the light aircraft took off from Earls Colne airfield in Essex at 2.48pm on Saturday and landed at 4.13pm, having spent around half an hour above the sea off Clacton, zig-zagging to create a flightpath in the shape of a bin. The plane is in private ownership according to Flightradar24 and it is not known who flew it during the stunt. Voters will go to the polls in Clacton on Thursday in a by-election triggered by the resignation Reform UK leader Mr Farage. Mr Farage is being investigated by the parliamentary standards commissioner Daniel Greenberg over a £5m gift from cryptocurrency tycoon Christopher Harborne, which he received before taking his seat in the Commons. The investigation, looking at whether he should have declared the money when he arrived in parliament, was suspended on his resignation, but is likely to resume if he wins the by-election. If he is found to have broken the rules and a suspension of more than 10 days is imposed, it could trigger a recall petition and the prospect of Mr Farage losing his seat, forcing a second contest. Mr Farage previously said he has “not broken the law in any way at all” and warned the standards probe was “now being used as a political tool”. The Reform leader had envisioned the contest as a "people versus the establishment" showdown, but he now finds himself up against a varied group, including three candidates from the Official Monster Raving Loony Party and numerous independents. All the main Westminster parties are boycotting the by-election and many have dismissed it as a “stunt”. Yvette Cooper called the move by Mr Farage a “political tantrum” and others said it was a “distraction” from allegations made about his financial affairs. And polls reveal that one in five people in Clacton would rather vote for Count Binface than Mr Farage. A survey by Survation for Mandate Research of voters in Clacton suggests Mr Farage would win 73 per cent of the vote , while his main rival, the satirical sci-fi character who is a by-election veteran, could sweep up an estimated 20 per cent of the vote. In an Ipsos poll asking the general public who they would vote for in a hypothetical head-to-head, a third (33 per cent) of British adults said they would prefer Count Binface to win the race, while only 21 per cent back the Reform UK leader. Meanwhile, the poll found 32 per cent wouldn’t want either of them to win and 13 per cent didn’t know who they would chose. The lengthy ballot paper is filled with numerous fringe candidates alongside Count Binface, including actor-turned-politician Laurence Fox - who could take 2 per cent of the votes according to a poll by Survation for Mandate Research. title: All Blacks team v Sharks: Five takeaways from Dave Rennie's 'power-packed' side as 'obvious choice' handed captaincy - Planet Rugby
content: Cam Roigard will provide impact off the bench while Luke Jacobson skippers the All Blacks against the Sharks. Following the announcement of the All Blacks side that will take on the Sharks in their Greatest Rivalry tour clash, here are our five takeaways from Dave Rennie’s selection. Rennie has called in a whole host of first team stars for the second fixture of the tour of South Africa, while two players are set to make their debuts off the bench. Seven players from the 23 that faced the Stormers – Sam Darry, Kyle Preston, Asafo Aumua, Caleb Clarke, Ollie Norris, Pasilio Tosi and Ethan Blackadder – get a second chance to impress. Darry, Preston, Aumua and Clarke, who all came off the bench in Cape Town, will start against the Sharks while the latter trio take up bench places. This tour, of course, is a balancing act of rotation and timing in terms of minutes and form, and this is again juggled by Rennie, with all roads leading to the series. That results in several big guns returning to the fold after missing the Stormers game, with Damian McKenzie, Jordie Barrett, Quinn Tupaea, Ruben Love, Luke Jacobson, Tupou Vaa’i, Fletcher Newell and Ethan de Groot just some of the starters in what is a solid team that is likely to make a statement against an under-strength Sharks. Indeed, the gulf in class on paper seems apparent as the Sharks are missing a clutch of Springboks who are currently on their way back to South Africa from Argentina. It’s a largely second-string side from JP Pietersen, with the big talking point being Ma’a Nonu’s inclusion on the bench – what a sublot that will be late in the game. Sharks team v All Blacks: Ma’a Nonu primed for debut as Springboks return for midweek clash Put simply, New Zealand should have far too much class for the Durbanites this Tuesday as we expect a handsome victory, with the backline especially set to cut loose. One hopes that is not the case for the sake of the spectacle, but it is hard to shake the concern for the hosts ahead of kick-off as New Zealand unleash their weapons. What a special moment it will be for Jacobson as he is handed the All Blacks captaincy for the first time, with his purple patch in the team moving to taller heights. The Chiefs stalwart has very much been a feature in Rennie’s XVs since the head coach began his tenure and certainly has warranted his spot, putting in mighty shifts. All Blacks team v Sharks: Luke Jacobson appointed captain and two debutants named as Dave Rennie calls in the big guns “Luke is the obvious choice to captain the team. He’s highly respected, has a great feel for the game and will lead through his actions,” said Rennie on his decision. It certainly is a feather in the cap of Jacobson, who packs down at openside in Durban in a power-packed back-row that includes Vaa’i and number eight Wallace Sititi. As mentioned, this is an impressive side named by Rennie, as several of the team that featured in the impressive Nations Championship campaign will trot out in Durban. There is a lot to like about combinations and box office talent, with the aforementioned back-row and a solid midfield pairing of Barrett and Tupaea catching the eye. Love’s return at 10 will be a fascinating watch as he and the backline spine looks to build on the solid foundations it laid in July. Also keep an eye out for deadly Fehi Fineanganofo as he looks to translate his Super Rugby Pacific try-scoring form to the international stage, as one of the Test wing jerseys remains up for grabs. Comment: All Blacks need not ‘worry’ after Springboks ‘escaped to victory’ against Argentina It’s not just the XV that should strike fear into Sharks supporters, as having prop Tosi, flanker Blackadder, scrum-half Cam Roigard, centre Timoci Tavatavanawai and wing Emoni Narawa in reserve ready to be unleashed will provide a serious injection of pace and power for the All Blacks, who should cut loose in the closing stages. It’s wise from Rennie to give Preston a start here over Roigard as the former has waited patiently to get decent minutes under his belt. Some have argued the Crusaders nine is unlucky to find himself behind Cortez Ratima in the All Blacks pecking order and Tuesday is an ideal opportunity to press his case for a Test shirt. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. Perhaps more importantly, it keeps Roigard in cotton wool, to a degree, as he’s only likely to feature in the closing 20-25 minutes when spaces open up. There is no doubt Roigard is a special talent and crucial to New Zealand’s hopes of a Greatest Rivalry series victory, and with news today breaking that Billy Proctor is ruled out of the tour due to an injury, that is perhaps a timely reminder for Rennie that managing minutes and replacing stars when possible has to be considered. READ MORE: Siya Kolisi injury update as Springboks face nervous wait ahead of Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series with All Blacks The All Blacks saw three players sin-binned in their victory over the Stormers. title: Is Arsenal v Borussia Dortmund on TV? How to watch pre-season friendly - The Independent
content: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in Arsenal 2-3 Borussia Dortmund: The Gunners unveiled Bruno Guimaraes but conceded some sloppy goals as they fell to a second consecutive pre-season defeat Arsenal suffered a second consecutive pre-season defeat ahead of the start of their Premier League title defence as clinical Borussia Dortmund won the Emirates Cup with a 3-2 victory. New signing Bruno Guimaraes was unveiled to the Arsenal fans before kick-off and there was a party atmosphere as the Gunners returned to the Emirates for the first time since lifting the Premier League title in May. Captain Martin Odegaard returned for the first time since the World Cup and Gabrel Magalhaes started in defence, but sharp finishes from the visitors’ Samuele Inacio and Konstantinos Karetsas left Arsenal two goals down before half-time. Arsenal were beaten 3-1 by Real Betis In Dublin on Wednesday and quickly found themselves trailing by the same scoreline when Joane Gadou bundled in from a corner moments after Ethan Nwaneri had pulled one back. Viktor Gyokeres gave Arsenal some late hope from the penalty spot before Arteta made further changes, introducing several players from the club’s academy. Gabriel Martinelli had the ball in the net in stoppage time but was given offside. Arteta’s team will be back in action against Como on Wednesday, their final pre-season fixture before facing Manchester City in the Community Shield in Cardiff next Sunday and Coventry City in their Premier League opener the following Friday. Follow live updates from Arsenal v Borussia Dortmund in the Emirates Cup, below Speaking after the 3-2 defeat to Borussia Dortmund, Mikel Arteta confirmed he will have all his squad together on Monday for the first time since the World Cup. That means the likes of Bukayo Saka and Declan Rice will be back in training, as well as Spain’s Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi. They will not be rushed back into action ahead of Arsenal’s final pre-season test against Como on Wednesday, but Bruno Guimaraes could be available for his debut ahead of Saturday’s Community Shield against Manchester City. With the news that Vinicius Jr will be staying at Real Madrid, there may be an opportunity on the left side of Arsenal’s attack for new arrival Christos Tzolis after all. Certainly, the 24-year-old Greek has hit the ground running in his bid to replace Leandro Trossard’s impact in north London and produced another couple of decisive attacking contributions in the defeat to Dortmund. This was a bright display from the former Club Brugge attacker. He combined an impressive defensive workrate, with some key moments of tracking back to cut out Dortmund counter-attacks, with an ability to beat his defender and create space around the box in the attacking third. A couple of flashes, in particular, showcased an ability to get the ball from out of his feet and deliver into the box. He set up Ethan Nwaneri’s goal in the second half with a sharp pull-back, then was in the right place to pop up in the box and win Arsenal’s penalty - converted by Victor Gyokeres. Tzolis also took a several of Arsenal’s set-pieces after Martin Odegaard’s 30-minute cameo was up, only that may not continue once he also has Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and even Bruno Guimaraes ahead of him in the queue. Still, this was another encouraging display from Arsenal’s only attacking recruit of the transfer window. While the Gunners are reported to be turning their attention to other star names - such as highjacking Liverpool’s bid for Paris Saint-Germain’s Bradley Barcola - Tzolis is currently winning the race with Gabriel Martinelli to start the season as the piece alongside Gyokeres and Saka in attack. Sure, it’s only pre-season, but Arsenal’s defensive performance in their last two outings is a concern ahead of the new campaign. Arsenal only conceded three goals once last season,  in a 3-2 defeat to Manchester United, but have now shipped in three in back-to-back games following defeats to Real Betis and Borussia Dortmund. The worry for Mikel Arteta is that he had what could be his starting back-four in place against Dortmund. While David Raya is yet to return, Arsenal started with Gabriel Magalhaes and Cristhian Mosquera at centre-back and Riccardo Calafiori and Ben White at full-back. Unless the champions turn to the market with William Saliba and Jurrien Timber injured, that’s as strong as Arsenal will be able to go over the first few weeks of the season. Dortmund were clinical in attack in the first half but Arsenal also afforded the visitors too much room. First, Samuele Inacio slipped off the back off Gabriel and had the run on Mosquera as he fired the early opener past Kepa Arrizabalaga. The 18-year-old winger Karetsas then curled a brilliant strike beyond Kepa to double Arsenal’s lead, but again the defending from Arteta’s side left too much space around the box. Real Betis also scored a stunner in midweek, but this was also the second game in a row where Arsenal conceded from a corner. After the near-post delivery was not cleared, Joane Gadou bundled in a sloppy and avoidable third for Dortmund. The fact that Arsenal switched off just a couple of minutes after Ethan Nwaneri had pulled one back will also be a source of frustration. Arsenal’s defensive record was outstanding last season but it needs to sharper up as the new campaign approaches. It’s Como on Wednesday. Too soon for the likes of Declan Rice and Bukayo Saka? At this stage, yes, but could Bruno Guimaraes make his debut in midfield? Then, it’s on to the Community Shield against Manchester City on Saturday. City won 3-1 against Atletico Madrid to round off their pre-season tour of Asia. After six penalties were scored in a row, Illan Meslier saved from Mathis Albert. Gabriel Jesus, Fabio Viera, Piero Hincapie and Gabriel Martinelli scored for Arsenal. Mikel Arteta’s side have practiced their spot-kicks. 100% from the spot. I suppose Arsenal could have a penalty shootout against Manchester City in the Emirates Cup, and its’s preparation for the season ahead. Illan Meslier gets an opportunity in goal during the shootout. An improved performance in the second half from Arsenal but conceding another sloppy goal cost them. Borussia Dortmund win the Emirates Cup and now Arsenal turn their attention to Wednesday’s final pre-season warm-up against Como. Gabriel Martinelli has the ball in the net but he’s given offside! Arsenal took a short corner and Jesus flicks to Martinelli, who then finishes under Alexander Meyer. But the assistant referee Sian Massey-Ellis, who is retiring after this game, raises her flag! There is no VAR to check. 90 mins: We’re into three minutes of stoppage time. Fabio Viera goes for the chip from 30 yards when he had Gabriel Martinelli as an option. Not sure what he’s up to there. 88 mins: Dortmund looking to waste some seconds from a throw-in. Come on, folks. title: All Blacks team v Sharks: Luke Jacobson appointed captain - Planet Rugby
content:
All Blacks back-row Luke Jacobson and head coach Dave Rennie (inset). All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie has rung the changes to his starting line-up and appointed Luke Jacobson as captain for their clash against the Sharks in Durban on Tuesday. After getting Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry tour off to a winning start against the Stormers in Cape Town on Friday night, Rennie has made 15 changes to his run-on side for the match against the Sharks. Rennie has named Jacobson as the All Blacks‘ leader, and he will pack down on the openside flank against the Sharks in an exciting back-row which also features Wallace Sititi and Tupou Vaa’i, who will line up at number eight and on the blindside flank respectively. There are also two potential debutants in New Zealand’s matchday squad with hooker Bradley Slater and loose forward Semisi Ta’eiloa set to make their All Blacks bows from the bench in Durban. Slater’s All Blacks career is off to a whirlwind start, with the 27-year-old flying in to join the squad just five days ago as a replacement for the injured George Bell. Meanwhile, seven players from the All Blacks side that clinched a 38-21 victory over the Stormers at the DHL Stadium have again been named in the matchday 23 for this second match of the tour. Hooker Asafo Aumua, lock Sam Darry, scrum-half Kyle Preston, and wing Caleb Clarke, who all came off the bench against the men from the Cape, will start against the Sharks. Front-row Pasilio Tosi, who started in the Stormers encounter, will provide impact from the bench, alongside fellow prop Ollie Norris and loose forward Ethan Blackadder, who get their second bench start of the tour. Josh Lord joins Darry in the second-row while Ruben Love lines up alongside Preston at fly-half as the starting halfback duo, and Fehi Fineanganofo (wing) and Damian McKenzie (full-back) will form an exciting back three with Clarke. The rest of the starting backline sees Jordie Barrett and Quinn Tupaea lining up as the centres while up front Aumua packs down alongside Fletcher Newell and Ethan de Groot, who are the two props. Dave Rennie responds to disciplinary concerns after All Blacks struggles in tour opener: ‘That’s our game nowadays’ Rennie is looking forward to Jacobson leading the team, and it will be a momentous occasion for the 29-year-old as it will be the first time that he captains the All Blacks. “Luke is the obvious choice to captain the team against the Sharks,” said the head coach. “He is highly respected, has a great feel for the game and will lead through his actions.” Rennie is also excited by the prospect of Slater and Ta’eiloa making their All Blacks debuts and expects a tough challenge from the Sharks. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. “Two more players will pull on the All Blacks jersey for the first time against the Sharks. On behalf of the whole squad, I want to congratulate Semisi and Bradley on achieving this very special milestone, and I know their family and friends will be incredibly proud,” he said. “The opening match gave the players a real introduction to the way that South African teams play and the Sharks will be no different. “With a short turnaround between games, today has been a big day of preparation. There is a lot of excitement in the group, with the majority of the squad about to play their first game of the tour.” New Zealand: 15 Damian McKenzie, 14 Fehi Fineanganofo, 13 Quinn Tupaea, 12 Jordie Barrett, 11 Caleb Clarke, 10 Ruben Love, 9 Kyle Preston, 8 Wallace Sititi, 7 Luke Jacobson (c), 6 Tupou Vaa’i, 5 Sam Darry, 4 Josh Lord, 3 Fletcher Newell, 2 Asafo Aumua, 1 Ethan de Groot

content: We have thousands of human-written stories, discussions, interviews and reviews from today through the past 20+ years. Find them here: August 9, 2026, 12:40 AM · One interesting thing about classical music is that we continue to play things that people played hundreds of years ago, and that makes historical recordings feel more relevant to our present lives. I was thinking about this today, as I listened with one of my students to a recording of Itzhak Perlman playing Kreisler's "Praeludium and Allegro," recorded in 1978. It's a go-to recording for me, something I have heard many times. She is currently learning the piece, and it was so fun for me to watch her and her father respond to Perlman's playing - they were totally wowed, which made me feel wowed anew! I've always felt fascinated by old recordings, and it might be one reason why I sought out a job at Northwestern University's Music Library when I was a student there. The library was a wonder, in a beautiful leg of the library with stained-glass windows and old architecture. We had thousands of long-playing records behind the counter, organized in order of acquisition, from oldest to newest. And I had access to them all! Out of curiosity, one day I hunted down the very oldest recording on the shelf, and if memory serves, it was "Rachmaninov Plays Rochmaninov," likely from the 1920s. Of course Rachmaninoff was a pianist, and there are likewise many classic recordings of violinists from a century ago. It remains remarkable to me that those of us who were born too late to hear them live can listen to performances by Kreisler, Heifetz, Milstein, Ysaye, Elman etc. A recording does not have to be a century old to be considered historic. One of my favorite go-to recordings is the nearly half-century old recording of the Houston Opera's 1977 production of "Porgy and Bess." It's simply my favorite, I still listen in awe of that production's dramatic singing and totally committed orchestra playing. What is the oldest go-to recording that you listen to, and for the vote, what year was it recorded? (If it's a new release of an old recording, go with the year of the original recording.) You are welcome to talk about recordings of violinists, but also any other historic recordings that you have, that are go-to, repeat-listen kinds of recordings for you. Let's share our favorites! August 9, 2026 at 06:08 AM · There might be some older ones I go back to, but the premier of the Bartok 2nd violin concerto, by Zoltan Szekely with the Concertgebouw Orchestra led by Willem Mengelberg, is an absolutely magical recording, and I haven't heard another that tops it. Unfortunately, the premier happened on March 23, 1939, so it slips between the cracks of the options in the poll. August 9, 2026 at 10:23 AM · Couldn't name the recordings or claim I listen to them often, but I have Caruso, Kreisler, McCormack, some early Menuhin and Heifetz. Leon Goossens (brilliant 1933 recording of Mozart's Oboe Quartet in F major, K. 370), Bach well-tempered - Fischer. August 9, 2026 at 01:01 PM · I often seek out Otto Klemperer's Beethoven symphonies with the original Philharmonia Orchestra; and Alfred Brendel seemed to channel Beethoven and Schubert. I don't know the Houston 'Porgy and Bess' but I have Simon Rattle's Glyndebourne recording, with Willard White as Porgy, and the rest of the cast is equally sensational. August 9, 2026 at 01:21 PM · I've got old 78 recordings that probably go back to the 1920's (among a few others), but my all-time favorite is the Francescatti/Ormandy 1950 recording of the Beethoven Violin Concerto. August 9, 2026 at 03:10 PM · LP re-releases of course.  Kreisler, his short pieces, 192?.  Beethoven S. 7, New York Phil. with Toscanini, that's before NBC orch.  One of the major improvements in recording quality was replacing acoustic/mechnical recording with the  first version of electrical recording, about 1927.  That is when we also get a big improvement in field recordings of folk music. Those old 78s can have a better clarity than the first version 33.3 LPs. August 9, 2026 at 03:42 PM · Lipatti playing Chopin Dinu Lipatti plays Chopin's Nocturne in D-Flat Major Op.27 No.2) August 9, 2026 at 03:42 PM · Unfortunately I don’t have the record anymore but I found the recording on YouTube. It is Heifetz playing the Vitali Chaccone, recorded in 1957. The record was a gift from my violin teacher in Berlin in 1983. I lost it sometime in a move or when my parents downsized. I have heard other recordings of the Chaccone but this one is by far my favorite. It’s probably more romantic and passionate than the original intent of the piece, but that’s what I love about it. August 9, 2026 at 03:48 PM · Enescu playing Bach, Voicu playing pretty much anything (Locatelli Sonata Op 2 No 6 arranged for violin by Ferdinand David is currently on repeat for its pure sound), Igor Oistrach playing the Campanella... August 9, 2026 at 05:23 PM · I have an original recording of George Szell and the Cleveland playing the Bartok Concerto for Orchestra, recorded in 1958. What always comes to mind when I listen to this recording, compared with other recordings of the Concerto for Orchestra from this era, is that Szell was the first conductor to fully understand what this complex and trail blazing orchestral work was about and how to actually bring it to life. Readers are welcome to disagree. I heard many interesting stories about Bartok and Szell when I lived in Cleveland so many years ago. My favorite, Szell was conducting a Cleveland premiere of a Bartok piano concerto with Bartok himself at the keyboard. Suddenly the inspiration for a bold new passage came to the pianist. He improvised the passage on the spot while the conductor and orchestra clung to the score in limbo, doing the best they could and happily at some point pianist and orchestra ended up in the same spot. August 9, 2026 at 05:29 PM · Christian, I really meant "1939 and before" so go ahead and vote in that category! August 9, 2026 at 05:33 PM · Karen, that is a great recording of the Vitali Chaconne - with organ, too! Heifetz's clarity is really striking. August 9, 2026 at 06:42 PM · From 1924: the Larghetto from the Spohr Duet, op. 67, no. 2 recorded by the Hungarian sisters Jelly d’Aranyi and Adila Fachiri. Their organ-like double stop playing is just amazing. One of the greatest duet recordings. Jelly d’Aranyi was the inspiration for the Ravel Tzigane and Bartok also composed pieces for her. For beauty of tone, see the film of Nathan Milstein playing the Mozart Adagio in E from a London studio in the 1950s. Laurie, you and your student would enjoy a film of Itzhak Perlman playing the Praeludium and Allegro for school children in Germany in 1984. Also, highly recommended is a film of that piece with the great Oscar Shumsky from a N.Y. recital in 1975. All of the above are currently available on YouTube. August 9, 2026 at 07:01 PM · Done, Laurie! (I was just being obnoxious). I second Paul's recommendation of Dinu Lipatti playing, well, anything. There are some recordings from the 20s of Paul/Pawel Kochanski, for example, playing the Brahms 3rd sonata with Rubinstein. Those are great! Unfortunately, there don't seem to be any recordings of him playing any Szymanowski - What I wouldn't give to hear his premier of the 2nd Concerto. There are also some great Cortot and Thibaud recordings as far back as the 20s. August 9, 2026 at 07:53 PM · How much just got lost from this thread? August 9, 2026 at 09:11 PM · I still listen to Elgar conducting Menuhin at the premiere of his vc, Szymon Goldberg and Lili Kraus doing Beethoven and Mozart violin sonatas, Goldberg and Hindemith doing the Mozart duos K.423 and 424, Feuermann doing the Dvorak cello concerto and Heifetz, Feuermann and Rubinstein doing the Archduke Trio.  These recordings all pre-date 1939 and are excellent. August 9, 2026 at 11:24 PM · The earliest classical recording on my shelf (and the earliest I listen to somewhat regularly) is Dennis Brain's 1954 recording of the Mozart horn concerti. All the earlier recordings I have are jazz. I don't have much from before 1990 in my classical collection. The other things I have are: Brain's recording of the Strauss horn concerti from 1956; the Bloch concerti grossi and Schelomo, conducted by Howard Hanson in 1959-60; the Szell Beethoven cycle from between 1957 and 1966; and the EMI disc of the Bach violin concerti recorded by Itzhak Perlman and Pinchas Zukerman at various times in the 1970s and 1980s; and Andras Schiff's 1986-87 recordings of Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier and Goldberg Variations. title: Trump Allies See Birthright Citizenship as Next Roe v. Wade - Newsweek
content: People React To SCOTUS Decision On Birthright Citizenship People React To SCOTUS Decision On Birthright Citizenship Socialist Kshama Sawant Says AOC’s and Progressives’ Strategy Isn’t Working ICE Is Back. Has Anything Changed? Ft. John Sandweg People React To SCOTUS Decision On Birthright Citizenship Weeks after the Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump's effort to end birthright citizenship through executive action, conservative activists are already looking beyond the courtroom defeat and toward a longer-term goal: shaping the judges who may one day revisit the issue. At a late-July gathering of conservative lawyers, immigration hawks and Trump allies in Washington, participants discussed ways to keep the birthright citizenship debate alive following the Supreme Court's June ruling. According to Politico, attendees argued that views on birthright citizenship should become a factor in evaluating future judicial nominees. The discussion comes weeks after the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump v. Barbara that children born in the United States to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present in the country are citizens at birth under the 14th Amendment, rejecting Trump's executive order limiting birthright citizenship. Trump's allies, however, have argued that the Citizenship Clause has been interpreted too broadly and that the court's decision should not end efforts to revisit the issue. Justice Clarence Thomas and Justice Samuel Alito both dissented from the ruling, with Thomas writing that he was not convinced the court's interpretation would "stand the test of time." That dissent has become a rallying point for conservatives seeking to continue the fight. The White House on Thursday unveiled new executive orders targeting birth tourism and other narrow categories it argues fall outside traditional birthright citizenship protections, underscoring that the administration is not retreating from the issue. The measures are expected to face legal challenges. Their rollout came just weeks after Trump vowed to continue pursuing the issue despite the Supreme Court ruling. At the gathering, Mike Davis, founder of the Article III Project, a conservative legal group that has championed Trump-era judicial priorities, argued that conservatives should focus on shaping the courts and elevating judges more receptive to challenges to the prevailing interpretation of birthright citizenship. Pointing to Justice Samuel Alito, who dissented from the court's birthright citizenship ruling, Davis said: "We need nine Alitos on the Supreme Court," according to Politico. Participants also discussed pursuing the issue through legal scholarship, conferences, law schools, legislation and future litigation. But the conversation around judicial nominees stood out because it suggests conservatives increasingly view the judiciary itself as the most important battleground. Rather than representing a new approach to judicial nominations, the proposal could make birthright citizenship a new litmus test for conservative legal activists. The idea of evaluating judges through the lens of a single constitutional issue is hardly new. For decades, conservatives closely examined judicial nominees' positions on abortion after Roe v. Wade. Questions about constitutional interpretation, unenumerated rights and judicial restraint became central features of confirmation battles long before the Supreme Court overturned Roe in 2022. Gun rights also became a key flashpoint after major Second Amendment rulings, while conservatives frequently scrutinized nominees' positions on religious liberty, administrative power and how much deference federal agencies should receive from courts. More recently, conservative legal groups have closely tracked nominees' views on administrative power, religious liberty and constitutional originalism. Activists discussing birthright citizenship appear to envision a similar strategy, using judicial appointments to influence the legal landscape over time rather than relying solely on legislation or executive orders. Many legal scholars argue that the conservative legal movement's long-running focus on judicial appointments helped shape a Supreme Court willing to revisit precedents that earlier generations considered settled. Some activists explicitly compared the birthright citizenship debate to the decades-long campaign against Roe v. Wade. Article III Project's Davis said the Supreme Court's ruling had effectively turned birthright citizenship into "the next Roe v. Wade" and suggested conservatives may spend years trying to reverse it. The comparison reflects a strategy used by conservatives for decades after Roe established a constitutional right to abortion, culminating in the Supreme Court's 2022 decision to overturn the precedent. That comparison is notable because the movement against Roe extended beyond lawsuits. It involved legal scholarship, state legislation, public advocacy campaigns, judicial nominations and efforts to influence legal education. Participants at the gathering suggested a similar roadmap for birthright citizenship, according to Politico. Even though the Supreme Court ruled against Trump, some proponents of restricting birthright citizenship argue the case helped move the issue into mainstream political debate. John Eastman, who has advocated for a narrower interpretation of birthright citizenship for years, told Politico that reaching the Supreme Court itself represented a significant milestone. "It was a success that we got as far as we did," Eastman said, adding that the conversation is now taking place among lawmakers, judges and ordinary Americans. Supporters of the movement believe heightened public attention, combined with legislative proposals and continued litigation, could gradually build support for their arguments even if they were unsuccessful in the most recent case. For now, the Supreme Court's ruling remains the controlling law. Children born in the United States continue to receive citizenship under the court's interpretation of the 14th Amendment, and legal experts expect Trump's latest executive actions to face fresh court challenges. But comments from conservative activists suggest many are already looking beyond those immediate battles. Rather than focusing exclusively on the next lawsuit or executive order, they appear increasingly interested in a longer-term project: shaping the lawyers, legal scholarship and judges who could influence how future courts view birthright citizenship. If that effort gains traction, debates over judicial nominees could eventually include a question that rarely surfaced in confirmation hearings a decade ago: whether the Constitution's Citizenship Clause means what courts have long said it means.

title: Argentina v Springboks: Five takeaways as world champions win despite nothing working - Planet Rugby
content:
Argentina's Pablo Matera tackled by Eben Etzebeth and an inset of Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus. Following the Springboks’ 17-10 victory over Argentina, here are our five takeaways from the clash in Buenos Aires. South Africa won 17-10 as they did everything in their power to look like a team playing the first game of a tour – which is exactly what they were. Rassie Erasmus made 13 changes from the 43-0 win over Wales. Siya Kolisi, Eben Etzebeth, Lood de Jager and Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu were all playing their first rugby of 2026, and the front five had never packed down together. There was no rhythm in anything they did; they were second best in the air, second best at the breakdown and second best in the loose. But they won anyway, and that is what world champions do when nothing is working. Erasmus said beforehand that he wanted a hard Test to get his returning players back into full swing. He got exactly what he asked for, and whilst he’ll be pleased at the result, his day was somewhat spoiled when Kolisi went off inside half an hour holding his left leg, a fortnight before the All Blacks arrive. Thomas du Toit went to ground at the first scrum of the match and Argentina had a penalty. They kicked to the corner, drove it, Matera carried off the tail and popped for Benjamín Grondona to go through the fold. Ten-three, and, much against pre-match perceived wisdom, the platform South Africa were supposed to own had handed the home side the lead. Nothing much else worked at close quarters either, much to their own frustration. Their maul was collapsed twice inside the Argentine 22 and Christophe Ridley stayed with the penalty each time, correctly, because the maul on each occasion was going nowhere slowly and lacked the snap and momentum we expect from the Boks. Their throw was stolen at a third attacking lineout and the exit that followed gave away seventy metres and finished with Aphelele Fassi calling a mark on his own line. Then Hanekom scored off a scrum that went straight through Tomás Rapetti on 63 minutes. But the simple maths is seven scrums, seven won. Argentina had two all night. When a side has no shape and no confidence, the eight-man shove is the one thing that needs neither, and, once again, that incredible set-piece is the reason South Africa are flying to Cape Town with a win. Springboks player ratings: Bomb Squad ‘saves’ Rassie Erasmus’ men’s blushes against brave Los Pumas as Cameron Hanekom shines Fassi and Cobus Reinach were the only starters kept from the Wales team. They were meant to hold the shape whilst thirteen changes settled around them, yet they were amongst the two least convincing Springboks on the pitch, and Feinberg-Mngomezulu, in unusually stuttering and sluggish mode, made it three. The kicking from nine and ten went long, past its own chase, over and over again. That turned every contest into a gift and Rodrigo Isgró took the lot. He and Ignacio Mendy were the best wing pairing in the match by a distance; Mendy made four clean breaks, more than anyone on either side, but to South Africa’s credit, they never fully managed to get around the proud Bok scramble. Feinberg-Mngomezulu attacked the gainline hard early, which answered the ankle question inside ten minutes. But for some reason, instead of running a backline, he chased the explosive option all night and looked indecisive doing it as a result. A Kolisi carrying sequence near the line broke down in a knock-on because nobody knew whether the ball was going tight or wide. Kolisi departed with a calf issue, but Feinberg-Mngomezulu carried 24 times, second only to Johan Grobbelaar, and Erasmus will wait anxiously for the news on his talisman. Santiago Carreras, a full-back wearing ten only because Tomás Albornoz is serving four matches, ran the game better than the man opposite him and, surprisingly, he also won more turnovers than any player on the field, also doubling back as an auxiliary full-back in defence to return SA kicks, something that the Boks really failed to exploit. Latest World Rugby rankings: Springboks retain top spot ahead of All Blacks Tests as Wales rise to two-year high He was captain by default, with Julián Montoya unavailable, and he played like a man who had taken that opportunity to remind all that, at 33, he’s still one of the absolute elite back rows of the modern game. In fact, there’s so much Springbok in Matera’s style, and it’s said that South Africa both fear and relish playing against South America’s finest flank forward. He carried off the tail of the maul to make Grondona’s try. He was in the middle of the goal-line stand that held André Esterhuizen up over the line in the second half. He beat more defenders than anyone in the match, six of them, and made 14 tackles with both his back-row partners already off. Then came the 50:22, off the weaker foot, from a position where Argentina had run out of any other way to get up the field. A 33-year-old injury-plagued flanker manufactured a lineout on the Springbok line in the 79th minute. Los Pumas got the penalty from it and went for the corner with a tap instead of a kick, backing the carriers they had left rather than a lineout drive without their locks. 17 phases later Ridley blew for the knock-on. Matera did everything a number six can do in a Test match and several things a number six cannot. The build-up was all about who Argentina did not have. No Montoya, no Marcos Kremer, no Santiago Chocobares, no Justo Piccardo, no Bautista Delguy, no Joaquín Oviedo, ten uncapped men in the squad and Albornoz banned for confronting Angus Gardner after the England Test. Felipe Contepomi leaves Buenos Aires with more than he arrived with. Francisco Moreno came out of Tarucas in Super Rugby Americas and held Boan Venter on debut at tighthead, save for one scrum. Grondona, on five caps, scored the try, forced an error on his own line off Kolisi, and was taken off on fifty minutes having emptied himself rather than having faded. Juan Penoucos went on at eight into the exact window South Africa picked a six-two bench for. Mendy and Isgró both shaded their opponents in the battle of the contestables. Guido Petti was enormous in the tight and called the lineout that stole the Springbok throw. He also gave away the no-arms penalty on his own line that gifted South Africa their best attacking platform of the first half, but he was still the best second row in the game. Australia come to Jujuy on 29 August and Mendoza on 5 September, and the Nations Championship restarts in Europe in November. Argentina now have players who have been examined at this level rather than merely named in a squad. All Blacks can forget about being ‘vaguely competitive’ against Springboks as New Zealand media slam performance versus Stormers This is the part Erasmus will look at hardest. Argentina pushed up off the line without ever rushing, shoulders tight, spacing intact, taking away South Africa’s time without leaving holes behind the front line for the long pass, a classic moderated push defence. It was beaten once in 80 minutes. Esterhuizen carried hard enough to make Faustino Sánchez Valarolo and Lucio Cinti bite, which took a defender off the far side and let Edwill van der Merwe get round the cover for the try that levelled it at the break. Van der Merwe finished with 101 running metres and most of them came from that one break. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. South Africa carried 146 times to Argentina’s 101 and had 62 per cent of the territory. They made six clean breaks from it. Ignacio Ruiz made 25 tackles and Joaquín Moro 24, the two highest counts in the game. At hooker, the outstanding Grobbelaar deserves better than he got from the night around him. He carried 26 times, more than any player on the field, and had a try disallowed for Marco van Staden being in touch. He is not the incumbent hooker, but his emergence in this game gives SA yet another deep layer of cover in their squad. Elrigh Louw got through 14 tackles, but neither he nor Van Staden made any case at all for the loose forward cover behind Pieter-Steph du Toit, and Jasper Wiese. Etzebeth played all eighty on his 142nd cap. Erasmus had six forwards on the bench and left his most experienced lock out there for the duration, which is not what a coach does in a warm-up he is enjoying, something that should tell all of the pressure Argentina applied all afternoon.
SA move on to host New Zealand, but they’ll need to be a lot better against the All Blacks, even with home advantage. READ MORE: Dave Rennie: Rassie Erasmus has done it for eight years, we’ve had two months © Planet Sport Limited 2026 • All Rights Reserved
